column3: Shares the plea to Moses and a claimed guidance, but its delaying inquiry lacks the plague-and-breach pattern.
Near-verbatim counterpart: under affliction they ask Moses to invoke his Lord by the covenant and promise compliance.
Contrasts their claimed readiness for guidance with refusal after recognizing the messenger and clear signs.
Repeats the petition to Moses through his Lord, without distress, covenant, or an ensuing broken pledge.
Begins the immediate Moses-to-Pharaoh mission whose rejected signs lead to the plea in 43:49.
Links divine calling with divine guidance, framing the claimed guidance in 43:49 as dependent on God.
Another petition to Moses through his Lord, but only a remote formal parallel.
Immediate sequel: once punishment is removed, the speakers break their implied pledge.
Joins calling to one's Lord with being on right guidance, though in an exhortatory rather than crisis setting.
A defiant people demand the promised consequence from a messenger, paralleling Pharaoh's hostile posture.
Direct narrative parallel: punishment is uncovered for a term and the people immediately violate their undertaking.
The charge that a manifest sign is magic illuminates the insulting address to Moses as a magician.
Shows a declared refusal to heed a call, only a broad contrast to their momentary claim of guidance.
Immediate context: Pharaoh's people laugh at the signs before distress makes them appeal to Moses.
Sets covenant-keeping as the criterion, contrasting the temporary pledge made under pressure.
Distinguishes a magician's contrivance from Moses's sign, clarifying the false label in 43:49.
Within the surah, truth is dismissed as magic, the same evasive naming used against Moses.
Shows even tangible revelation being recategorized as manifest magic to avoid its claim.
Explicitly defines breaking a pledged covenant as self-harm, sharpening the breach that follows 43:49.
A servant calls his Lord in harm and receives relief, a sincere counterpart to the pressured appeal.
Treats covenant dissolution as a consequence of a failed binding relationship, not a mere spoken claim.
Models a responsive appeal to the Lord grounded in hearing the call to faith, unlike their expedient pledge.
Immediate prior verse: escalating signs and punishment were intended to bring Pharaoh's people back.
Makes covenant continuity conditional on reciprocal steadfastness, exposing the weakness of their conditional promise.
A believing plea to the Lord contrasts with the crisis-driven profession of guidance in 43:49.
Its local oath by the clear Book contributes only the surrounding surah's truth-claim context.
Presents people who remain true to what they pledged to God, the inverse of Pharaoh's people after relief.
Hostile hearers demand punishment if the message is true, a close pattern of defiant response to revelation.
Relief follows a faithful servant's invocation to his Lord, contrasting the later breach in the Pharaoh narrative.
Another messenger is dismissed as bewitched, showing the polemical use of magic language to evade warning.
Places Moses before the feared tyranny of Pharaoh, supplying the mission setting behind the later exchange.
The surah's challenge to inherited authority is only a secondary backdrop to Pharaoh's conditional claim.
Defines the Quran as guidance for believers, contrasting a profession of guidance without durable belief.
Pairs calling to the Lord's way with God's knowledge of the rightly guided, limiting their self-description.
Uncovering a veil concerns final disclosure, only distantly related to punishment being uncovered.
Repeats the charge that a messenger is bewitched, another strategy for dismissing his warning.
Names the Lord and right speech, but does not engage Moses, relief, or a conditional profession.
The surah's straight-path command supports the guidance theme but is not tied to the plague episode.
Guidance is withheld from entrenched transgressors, challenging a verbal claim made without change.
Finds most prior communities lacking any covenant, directly foreshadowing the unreliability of their pledge.
Affirms that no rival can remove harm God decrees, identifying the real source of the relief they seek.
Calls revelation inherited magic, a compact parallel to the misnaming of Moses in 43:49.
Rejecters call Moses's given signs magic despite demanding comparable proof, closely matching Pharaoh's evasion.
Local retribution after denial belongs to the surah's warning pattern but adds little to the specific plea.
Uses calling for the summons of Hell, with no meaningful route to the appeal to Moses.
Opponents privately reduce the messenger to a bewitched man, paralleling the discrediting label applied to Moses.
Shows that belief can lead to punishment being removed, the substantive response absent after 43:49.
Contrasts guided and rebellious descendants, but provides no direct plea, covenant, or relief relation.
The saved credit God for guidance, contrasting the Pharaoh group's unfulfilled assertion that they are guided.
Another local false assertion in the surah, but it does not develop the Moses episode.
Pharaoh and his court explicitly call Moses a magician and liar, directly explaining the address in 43:49.
Shows hearers who listen yet leave without understanding, a contrast to a merely situational declaration of belief.
Names God as the one who answers the distressed and removes evil, the source behind the requested relief.
Denies that lesser objects of invocation control anything, reinforcing why appeal must ultimately be to the Lord.
Even overwhelming signs do not produce belief in the unwilling, explaining why repeated signs did not reform them.
Immediate surah parallel: they call inherited custom guidance, another unsupported claim to being rightly guided.
Pharaoh charges Moses with magic and treats his mission as a threat, framing the hostility beneath 43:49.
A conditional pledge to God under hoped-for benefit anticipates the failure of commitment once the condition passes.
A stricken people ask their Lord to remove punishment and profess belief, closely paralleling the crisis plea.
A messenger persistently calls his people, reversing the direction of the people calling Moses in distress.
Pharaoh's wife sincerely invokes her Lord for rescue from Pharaoh, sharply contrasting her household's response.
A lasting word is preserved so that people may return, supporting the surah's repeated call to genuine return.
Pharaoh's people pre-classify every sign as magic and refuse belief, directly exposing the stance behind 43:49.
Moses trusts that his Lord will guide him, a faithful counterpart to the people's asserted guidance.
God announces a brief removal of punishment followed by their return, the exact temporary-relief pattern.
The messenger calls people to believe in their Lord while recalling an existing covenant, joining call, faith, and pledge.
Assigns guidance to God, qualifying the people's claim that they themselves will be guided.
Immediate background: truth and a clarifying messenger came before the local rejection that frames the episode.
A call to powerless objects for guidance cannot be answered; it is only a broad inversion of 43:49's appeal.
Pharaoh's magicians genuinely believe in their Lord and renounce their compelled magic, a decisive contrast.
Moses invokes his Lord against a criminal people, extending the same Moses-and-distress sequence in Surah 44.
Uses the verb call for a hopeless cry in punishment, without a covenant or guidance connection.
The saved praise God for removing sorrow, a grateful response unlike the Pharaoh group's breach after relief.
The surah's final return to God adds only a distant accountability frame to the incident.
Connects undiluted faith with security and guidance, countering their unsupported claim of being guided.
Praises fulfillment of the Lord's promise, with only a loose relation to their appeal by a covenant.
States that even mercy and removal of harm can leave people persisting blindly in transgression.
Public calling to good is a general guidance theme, not a direct relation to the pressured pledge.
A people accuse a messenger of turning them from their gods and demand the threatened consequence.
The local return to the Lord supplies only broad surah context for their claim of future guidance.
Pharaoh mobilizes expert magicians against Moses, explaining the court's effort to frame his signs as magic.
Demanding a sign from the Lord despite existing proof parallels refusal to learn from Moses's repeated signs.
States unequivocally that only God can remove harm, the theological premise of their request to Moses's Lord.
Challenges an asserted covenant with God that lacks warrant, paralleling reliance on a pledge without fidelity.
Unbelievers condition belief on a demanded sign, a related pattern of transactional response to revelation.
In the same surah, the Creator alone is named as the one who will guide, correcting false claims of guidance.
Clear signs accompany God's guidance by will, relating proof to the source of genuine guidance.
The magicians' oath by Pharaoh situates the rival magical establishment confronting Moses.
Affirms that God's guidance cannot be overturned, contrasting the instability of their pledged guidance.
False objects once invoked disappear from account, a remote warning about misdirected invocation.
Worldly enjoyment as a test is only an indirect background to Pharaoh's resistance.
Forbids invoking another god with God, reinforcing the exclusive divine orientation of Moses's prayer.
Calls people to worship the one Lord shared by the messenger and audience, unlike a merely expedient appeal.
A messenger cannot make the blind see or guide those without inner sight, limiting Moses's intermediary role.
The Book is a mercy from the Lord, but the verse does not develop the plea or its aftermath.
A call to peace under military pressure is not materially related to the request for plague relief.
Final disclosure of deeds supplies only a distant accountability horizon for their broken promise.
Directly depicts calling God in distress, then passing on after relief as though no plea had been made.
Repentance and faith after wrongdoing lead to mercy, supplying the genuine alternative to their temporary profession.
Its destructive guidance to punishment is a lexical contrast, not a route to the Pharaoh episode.
Pharaoh's appeal to territorial power follows the failed signs and explains the political resistance behind the plea.
His demand for visible superiority over Moses continues the court's effort to discredit God's messenger.
The demand for ornaments or angels shows the material criteria by which Pharaoh's court rejects Moses.
Pharaoh manipulates his people into obedience, explaining why their crisis profession never becomes settled guidance.
The narrative concludes that their persistent provocation led to retribution, completing the breach-to-punishment sequence.
Their destruction is made a precedent for later hearers, extending the warning embodied in 43:49-50.
Pharaoh's chiefs identify Moses as a knowledgeable magician, an exact parallel to the address in 43:49.
They portray Moses's message as a threat of expulsion, exposing the political motive beneath the magic charge.
The chiefs seek delay and gatherers for magicians, beginning the institutional response to Moses's signs.
The summons of expert magicians shows how the court attempts to answer revelation with managed spectacle.
The magicians' demand for reward reveals the courtly interests aligned against Moses.
Pharaoh's promise of proximity makes the magic contest an instrument of patronage and power.
The magicians temporarily bewitch the spectators, distinguishing their craft from Moses's sign.
Moses's staff invalidates the magicians' fabrication, directly refuting the label applied to him in 43:49.
The magicians' prostration marks recognition that Moses's sign is not magic.
Their confession of faith in the Lord of the worlds is the genuine guidance Pharaoh's people only profess under pain.
Pharaoh calls the magicians' faith a plot, continuing his refusal to accept the sign's meaning.
The believing magicians invoke their Lord for patience after recognizing the truth, a sincere counterpart to 43:49.
Years of drought and reduced produce begin the pressure that eventually produces the plea for relief.
Pharaoh's people attribute good fortune to themselves and blame Moses for adversity, preparing their refusal to learn.
The successive plagues provide the immediate affliction whose removal they seek in 43:49's parallel episode.
After denial and heedlessness, Pharaoh's people are drowned, completing the warning after repeated signs and failed pledges.
When truth comes through Moses, Pharaoh's people call it manifest magic, directly paralleling 43:49.
Moses challenges the magic accusation and distinguishes truth from magic, clarifying the false address in 43:49.
They accuse Moses and Aaron of seeking to displace inherited authority, exposing their political resistance.
Pharaoh gathers every skilled magician as an organized countermeasure against Moses.
Moses declares that God will nullify the magicians' work, directly distinguishing the sign from magic.
Only a few believe in Moses because of fear of Pharaoh and his chiefs, explaining the coercive setting.
Moses invokes God against Pharaoh and his chiefs after their wealth and power have turned people from the way.
God answers Moses and Aaron's prayer while commanding steadfastness, the faithful inverse of a temporary crisis plea.
Pharaoh proposes a public magic contest against Moses, making explicit the charge repeated in 43:49.
The assembled magicians describe Moses and Aaron as magicians threatening established rule and inherited order.
They are told to unite their stratagem, showing coordinated resistance rather than open assessment of the signs.
The magicians believe on seeing the decisive sign, contrasting real recognition with Pharaoh's people's opportunism.
Pharaoh recasts their faith as a conspiracy, preserving the same evasive interpretive frame.
Pharaoh calls Moses a learned magician before his chiefs, an especially close verbal parallel.
He portrays Moses as seeking expulsion, again showing the political function of the magic accusation.
The chiefs advise postponement and collecting magicians, continuing the official counter-strategy.
The magicians seek reward before contesting Moses, showing their dependence on Pharaoh's interests.
Moses lets the magicians begin, setting the contrast between their performance and the divine sign.
The magicians confess faith in the Lord of Moses and Aaron, the authentic response to the signs.
Pharaoh treats their faith as unauthorized plotting, refusing the evidence rather than answering it.
The magicians hope for forgiveness after belief, a lasting commitment unlike the pledge in 43:49.
When Moses brings clear signs, Pharaoh's people call them fabricated magic and deny them.
Pharaoh denies knowledge of any god but himself and commissions a monument, exposing the rival sovereignty at stake.
After Moses brings truth, Pharaoh orders violence against believers' sons, showing the coercion behind public denial.
Pharaoh again calls Moses a threat to religion and order, the governing logic behind his court's accusations.
Moses seeks refuge in his Lord from every arrogant denier of the accounting, contrasting Pharaoh's arrogance.
The question of how they can receive the reminder after a clear messenger came exposes their belated crisis profession.
They turned away from the messenger and called him taught and mad, a close counterpart to calling Moses a magician.
A greater seizure is promised after their return, completing the temporary-removal warning of 44:15.
The Surah 44 counterpart explicitly introduces Pharaoh's people as tested before the plea for lifted punishment.
Moses commands Pharaoh's people to deliver God's servants, grounding the conflict in their refusal of his mission.
Moses warns them not to exalt themselves against God, naming the arrogance that blocks their response.
Moses seeks his Lord's protection from their threatened violence, continuing the invocation motif.
His demand that they leave him alone if they will not believe makes clear that their refusal precedes punishment.
God commands Moses to depart with His servants by night, following the Pharaoh narrative's final rejection.
Pharaoh's army is left to pursue into the sea, setting up the definitive consequence of their refusal.
Pharaoh is named as arrogant and excessive, characterizing the leadership that steers the people from guidance.
Moses comes to Pharaoh with clear authority, the basis for the court's later refusal and accusation.
Pharaoh turns away in his power and calls Moses a magician or madman, directly matching 43:49's polemic.
Warnings came to Pharaoh's people before their punishment, supplying the wider warning-and-rejection pattern.
They deny all the signs, explaining why affliction and a momentary plea do not become durable faith.
Moses receives clear signs for Pharaoh, tying the episode to a defined body of evidence.
Moses tells Pharaoh he knows the signs came from the Lord, directly confronting his knowing denial.
Moses and Aaron are sent with signs and clear authority to Pharaoh and his chiefs.
Pharaoh and his chiefs respond with arrogance, refusing to believe in the two human messengers.
Their refusal rests on social superiority and fear of losing control, echoing the court's political resistance.
Moses is sent to Pharaoh because he has transgressed, naming the tyrant's moral condition behind the episode.
Moses's invitation to purification provides the positive alternative to Pharaoh's destructive response.
Moses shows Pharaoh the great sign, the evidentiary basis repeatedly dismissed as magic.
Pharaoh denies and disobeys after the sign, encapsulating the rejection that 43:49 temporarily interrupts.
Pharaoh's supreme-lord claim directly opposes the appeal to Moses's Lord in 43:49.
Moses is sent to Pharaoh and his chiefs with signs and clear authority.
They follow Pharaoh's command rather than Moses's signs, explaining the collective failure to be guided.
Pharaoh leads his people into the Fire, the final inversion of his leadership after their rejected guidance.
